issues.issue: The 30-class-day hearing deadline is immediately qualified by "or as soon as practicable," which leaves the promised timing without any enforceable limit. The bar on the parties "confronting or questioning the witnesses and accusers... prior to the hearing" is also unbounded in scope and duration.

19.6 says the hearing administrator is non-voting and "will not act in any way to inuence the outcome of a case," which cannot be squared with Section 23.P.1, under which the administrator advises the Board of the accused's past conduct during deliberations, or with 20.11's duty to advise the Board at all stages. The administrator's role is described two incompatible ways.

19.7 lets "the accused and accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while 20.2 permits waiver of the voting requirements only "by mutual consent of the SCB, the accuser, and the accused." The two provisions specify different consenting parties for the same waiver.

"Passive assistance" is nowhere defined, and the exception permitting "active participation" in "exceptional circumstances" is left to the hearing administrator without criteria. What an adviser may actually do at a hearing is therefore indeterminate.

19.8 makes the passive assistance of legal counsel something that "may be allowed," whereas the Section 3 services statement tells students that this section "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel" whenever parallel criminal charges are pending. The instrument states the same entitlement as both discretionary and as of right.

19.9 says the accuser "must be present at the hearing," but the instrument supplies a consequence only for the accused's absence (19.15 deems acceptance of responsibility) and nowhere states what happens if the accuser does not appear. Read with 19.11's receipt of written testimony from absentee witnesses, the mandatory-presence rule has no ascertainable effect.

19.10 says "the Board shall rule on the admissibility of evidence and any witness testimony" and cross-references 19.6, which instead commits additional or unlisted witnesses "to the discretion of the chairperson of the Board." Who decides what evidence comes in is answered two ways.

The provision guarantees the right to question all witnesses "appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" while in the next breath allowing written testimony from absentee witnesses that by definition cannot be questioned. The right to question and the receipt of untested written statements are stated together without reconciliation.

Placing the "burden of proof" on the accuser cannot be squared with 19.1 and 19.15, which deem responsibility accepted when the accused misses a deadline or a hearing, or with 18.0, under which the University and not the accuser prosecutes the charge. The provision also does not say whether the burden is one of production or persuasion.

The body of 19.13 permits a finding of responsibility "based only upon clear and convincing evidence" while the appended Note substitutes preponderance of the evidence for Section 3 and 7 cases, so the provision states two standards of proof in one breath. Which governs a case charging both a Section 3 violation and other misconduct is unaddressed.

"All decisions shall be made by a majority vote" with the chairperson voting "only to break a tie" cannot be worked with 20.2's four-member academic-integrity panel and 20.5's rule that the SCB is chaired by students. Whether the student chair is one of the required student voters is left unresolved.

The retention sentence is internally inconsistent (five years from the hearing, then five years from the last conduct action) and its parenthetical — "(except in extraordinary cases as dened by the Dean of Student Life (see Section 19.5)." — is unclosed and garbled. The actual destruction date cannot be derived from the text.

Deeming an absent student to "have accepted responsibility" cannot be squared with 19.12, which places the burden of proof on the accuser, or with 19.13, which requires decisions to rest solely on evidence introduced at the hearing. Responsibility is established by non-attendance rather than proof.

Appeals lie only on "specic evidence, presented in writing" of fraud, "denial of rights under this process," procedural error, or new evidence — terms that are undefined and that exclude any challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence. "Denial of rights under this process" in particular has no stated content.

19.16 promises that a meritorious appeal produces "a new hearing of the case" before the UAB, yet 20.8 constitutes the UAB as a three-member review body and Section 23 prescribes hearing procedures only for the SCB. What a UAB "new hearing" consists of cannot be determined from the instrument.

The student has only "2 class days" from delivery of the announcement to request the meeting, and the Dean "may or may not amend" the decision under no stated standard. The review is thus a right without criteria and with a deadline running from delivery rather than receipt.

19.18 directs students to seek a continuance rather than raise a matter for the first time on appeal, which sits against 19.16.d's express appeal ground of "new evidence not previously available." Whether information glimpsed at the hearing is forfeited as an appeal ground is left to construction.

The provision says the governing procedures are those "enumerated in Section 19" but also those "available in the Department... or on the website," without saying which controls if they diverge. An off-document source is given equal standing with the handbook.

20.2 allows the mandatory panel composition to be waived only "by mutual consent of the SCB, the accuser, and the accused," whereas 19.7 allows "the accused and accuser" alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum composition. The two waiver rules cannot both be applied.

"Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" omits its verb, leaving it unclear whether the appointment is mandatory or merely descriptive. The provision also does not say how large the pool must be.

"A process open to all continuing students" and "a representative cross-section of Brandeis students" state no selection criteria or method, and the second sentence is syntactically scrambled. Whether a panel is properly constituted cannot be tested against these words.

"Chaired by students, each annually selected by the Board and the DSRCS Director" does not say how many chairpersons there are or how a disagreement between the Board and the Director is resolved. The plural chairs also complicate 19.13's tie-breaking rule for "the chairperson."

Removal turns on "behavior that conicts with the high standards of citizenship, condentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents," a standard with no defined content and no process. Any removal decision is effectively unreviewable on these words.

20.7 provides that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as chairperson of the University Appeals Board," which cannot be squared with 20.8's requirement that "A chairperson who is a full-time tenured faculty member shall be appointed by the Dean of Student Life." The two consecutive provisions name incompatible chairs.

20.8 requires a full-time tenured faculty chairperson appointed by the Dean, while 20.7 states that an Associate Dean of Student Life will chair the UAB. Which officer presides over an appeal is left in direct conflict.

Students appointed to the Appeals Board "must be free from all elected, appointed, or afliate relationships with the Student Union or Graduate Student Association," yet the same provision has them appointed to the voter pool by the Presidents of those very bodies. The eligibility bar and the appointment mechanism work against each other.

"Selected in a manner similar to that of the SCB" imports an undefined degree of similarity to a process (20.4) that is itself unspecified. "The original appointing authority" is also ambiguous where the chair is appointed by the Dean but faculty by the Faculty Senate chair.

Removal requires consultation with "the chairperson," whose identity is itself disputed as between 20.7 and 20.8, and rests on the undefined "high standards of citizenship, condentiality, and cooperation." Neither the actor nor the standard is fixed by the text.

20.11 requires a Student Affairs administrator to be present "in all stages of the conduct process including hearings and deliberations" and to advise the Board on requirements, procedures and sanctions, which cannot be squared with 19.6's statement that the administrator "will not act in any way to inuence the outcome of a case." The same officer is given advisory power and told to have none.

The sanctioning factors are "including but not limited to" and the learning components "may include but are not limited to" a list that mixes education with "Failure in a course or on an assignment," "Restitution for damages," and "Family notication." Neither the factors nor the permissible components have any boundary.

21.1 makes sanctions effective only on approval by the Director or Associate Dean "who can modify the sanction," while 19.16 contemplates approval or modification by the Dean or the Director before appeal and empowers the UAB to increase or decrease the sanction thereafter. Who may finally set a sanction, and in what order, is stated inconsistently.

The sanction is titled "Verbal Warning" but the text describes no warning at all — only that "further action may not be deemed necessary" while the responsible finding is recorded. Whether a verbal warning is a sanction with record consequences is left ambiguous.
"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" places no limit on what may be attached to a written warning. The sanction is therefore open-ended despite being the second-lowest on the scale.

"Not in good standing with their living unit" is undefined and carries no stated consequence, and "conditions may be placed on their actions" is unbounded. The content of residence probation cannot be read off the provision.

"Such action would normally be taken after one serious violation or repeated violations" states a norm, not a rule, and "serious" is undefined. The provision does not say who decides or whether departure from the norm is permitted.
The privileges that may be withdrawn are "including, but not limited to" an enumerated list, so any University benefit could be swept in. "A specic period of time" is required but no maximum is set.

Probation may be revoked if the student violates its terms "or in any way fail[s] to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community" — a condition with no ascertainable content. Suspension or dismissal can follow on that undefined trigger.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certicates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is garbled and, as written, states no third alternative duration. The maximum length of a suspension cannot be determined from the text.

The University may act whenever it "has reason to believe" behavior "may pose a signicant threat" and may then "take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable," with the enumerated examples expressly non-exclusive. Neither the trigger nor the permissible response has a stated limit.

22.1 authorizes removal on a "signicant threat" standard, while 22.2 provides that pending final action a student's status "shall not be altered" or campus presence suspended "except for reasons of imminent danger." The two adjacent provisions set incompatible thresholds for the same interim removal.

22.2's protection against alteration of status absent "imminent danger" cannot be squared with 22.1 ("signicant threat"), 22.3 (removal on a criminal charge), or 2.1.f and 3.0, which allow emergency suspension of any student merely accused pending investigation. The instrument states at least three different triggers for the same interim measure.

22.3 permits indefinite suspension on a mere criminal charge and declares that "the procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply," which cannot be squared with 18.0's rule that discipline may be implemented "only though referral" to the DSRCS or with 22.2's imminent-danger limit. A student can be removed indefinitely with none of the process the handbook otherwise promises.

Discipline up to dismissal turns on off-campus behavior that "in the judgment of the Dean" is inconsistent with being a "good citizen[] and good neighbor[]" and "adversely affects the University community." Those standards are undefined and committed wholly to one officer's judgment.

22.4 states that "the procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" to a Dean's Sanction, which cannot be squared with 19.16's guarantee of appeal to the University Appeals Board from decisions imposing sanctions, or with 18.0's requirement of DSRCS referral. A dismissal may thus issue with no hearing and no appeal.

"Emergency protocol" is nowhere defined, yet it bars the student from all campus property and classes with "no exception for examinations or other time-sensitive... academic obligations" until the Dean gives written permission. The provision fixes no duration and no standard for lifting the protocol.

The chairperson explains a "philosophy of peer judgment" contained in a separate statement "available from the Department," a document not reproduced in the handbook. What that statement says, and whether it binds the Board, is outside the instrument.

The right "to question witnesses appearing against them" cannot be squared with 19.11, which permits the Board to receive written testimony from absentee witnesses who never appear. The stated right of confrontation is defeated by the evidentiary rule elsewhere in the instrument.

The sentence is scrambled: "bring them into the hearing room either individually or as a group for descriptions of the incident in alphabetical order" does not say whether alphabetical order governs the grouping, the descriptions, or both. "This system shall prevail throughout the remainder of the hearing procedures" then locks in whichever reading is taken.
